claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC structure.
The initial high-temperature BCC material is fully homogenized.
Cooling the high-temperature BCC state causes nanoscale local chemical ordering to emerge.
The proposed local chemical ordering selectively enriches Cr and Al.
Local chemical ordering lowers the local free energy.
Local chemical ordering acts as a structural seed for nucleation of ordered secondary phases.
Subsequent thermal exposure can produce B2-type or other ordered intermetallic phases from the locally ordered regions.
Slow cooling or suitable isothermal holds provide enough time for local chemical order to develop.
An extreme quench kinetically suppresses the atomic rearrangements needed for local chemical ordering.
Local chemical ordering can be associated with evolving precipitate-boundary configurations or ordered boundary regions.
Atomic mobility during cooling enables subtle elemental partitioning.
Sluggish diffusion inherent to high-entropy alloys competes with ordering and partitioning.
Slow-cooled or isothermally aged specimens will contain more nanoscale chemical order than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled or isothermally aged specimens will contain more secondary ordered phases than rapidly quenched specimens.
Rapidly quenched specimens will largely retain a homogeneous BCC phase with minimal nanoscale chemical order.
Thermal exposure outside a temperature range permitting appreciable atomic reordering will not cause the proposed transition.
Very high temperatures can homogenize and remove the proposed ordering.
The relative roles of magnetic fluctuations and chemical ordering in phase stability are not established.
The degree of order and identity of secondary phases produced under different thermal histories remain unquantified.
